text:
PREMISE: Billionaires had a normal year.

STEP 1: Forbes: the 400 richest Americans were worth a record $8 trillion in September 2026, up from $6.6 trillion a year earlier.
STEP 2: That's a $1.4 trillion gain, about 21%, in one year.
STEP 3: Over the same stretch, average hourly pay rose 3.0% and prices 3.4%.
STEP 4: Their wealth grew about seven times faster than paychecks.

CONCLUSION: It wasn't a normal year. It was a record year at the top and a pay cut at the bottom.

PREMISE: It's getting easier for regular people to get rich.

STEP 1: The minimum to make the Forbes 400 hit a record $4.4 billion in 2026, up $600 million in a year.
STEP 2: A full-time worker at the average $37.81 an hour earns about $78,600 a year.
STEP 3: At that pay, earning $4.4 billion would take about 56,000 years.
STEP 4: At Louisiana's $7.25 floor, it would take about 292,000 years.

CONCLUSION: The ladder isn't getting shorter. The top rung is moving away.

PREMISE: Billionaires are a handful of people. They don't matter to the economy.

STEP 1: Forbes counted a record 989 U.S. billionaires in March 2026.
STEP 2: By September, about 990 Americans were billionaires: 400 on the Forbes 400 and 590 more too 'poor' to make it.
STEP 3: The Forbes 400 alone held about $8 trillion.
STEP 4: Fed data put the bottom half of U.S. households at about $4.3 trillion in Q2 2026.

CONCLUSION: Four hundred people hold roughly twice what half the country holds (different methods, same picture). That matters.
sources: Federal Reserve DFA via FRED, Q2 2026

text:
PREMISE: Everyone's wealth went up, so everyone's winning.

STEP 1: Concede it: the bottom half's net worth rose about 7% in a year, to $4.3 trillion.
STEP 2: The top 1% gained about $8.75 trillion in the same year, to $60.3 trillion.
STEP 3: That's more than 30 times the bottom half's dollar gain.
STEP 4: The top 1%'s share rose to 32.5%. The bottom half's fell to 2.3%.

CONCLUSION: Both grew. One grew 30 times more. Report the percent and the dollars.
sources: Federal Reserve DFA via FRED, Q2 2026

text:
PREMISE: Elon Musk's wealth is just a number. It doesn't affect anyone.

STEP 1: Forbes put Musk at $908 billion in September 2026, the most ever on the list.
STEP 2: He briefly passed $1 trillion during SpaceX's June IPO.
STEP 3: That's about 10 million years of the median household's income ($87,460).
STEP 4: Wealth on that scale buys media platforms, political influence and government contracts.

CONCLUSION: A fortune that size isn't just a number. It's power, and power affects everyone.

PREMISE: Billionaire net worths are exact facts.

STEP 1: Forbes and others estimate fortunes from stock prices and private valuations.
STEP 2: Musk was about $1.285 trillion in June per an advocacy group's tally of Forbes data, and $908 billion in September per Forbes.
STEP 3: Paper wealth can swing hundreds of billions in a few months.
STEP 4: The estimates differ by source and date.

CONCLUSION: Always give the source and the date. The exact number moves. The gap doesn't.

PREMISE: The billionaire boom is just good luck in the stock market.

STEP 1: Forbes tied much of the 2026 gain to the AI and data center boom and stocks near record highs.
STEP 2: Forbes counted at least 86 AI-linked billionaires in March 2026.
STEP 3: The same year, workers' share of business income hit a record low, 52.8%.
STEP 4: When profits and stock values rise faster than pay, owners win by design, not luck.

CONCLUSION: It's not luck. It's who owns the assets that rise.

PREMISE: Billionaires pay a lot in taxes.

STEP 1: Many pay large dollar amounts. Concede that.
STEP 2: But most billionaire wealth is unsold stock. Gains aren't taxed until sold.
STEP 3: A 2021 White House study estimated the 400 richest families paid about 8.2% of income including unrealized gains (estimate).
STEP 4: A cashier pays 7.65% in payroll taxes on every dollar, before income tax.

CONCLUSION: Big checks, small rates. Measure taxes against what they gain, not what they report.

PREMISE: If billionaires paid more, it wouldn't make a dent.

STEP 1: The Forbes 400 gained about $1.4 trillion in one year.
STEP 2: Federal food and nutrition programs cost about $137 billion in FY2026.
STEP 3: Federal Medicaid spending was about $723 billion.
STEP 4: One year of their gains is about ten times the food budget and about twice federal Medicaid.

CONCLUSION: It's not a dent. Even a slice of one year's gains could fund what Congress cut.

PREMISE: We can't afford SNAP, but the economy is booming.

STEP 1: SNAP enrollment fell 5.3 million from June 2025 to June 2026.
STEP 2: Food and nutrition spending fell $11 billion in FY2026.
STEP 3: Over a similar year, the Forbes 400 gained $1.4 trillion.
STEP 4: The money exists. It moved up, not out.

CONCLUSION: Hunger isn't a shortage of money. It's a choice about where money goes.

PREMISE: Taxing unrealized gains is unfair. You shouldn't pay tax on money you don't have.

STEP 1: Steelman: unsold stock can fall. Taxing it every year raises real valuation problems.
STEP 2: But billionaires borrow against that stock to live, without selling.
STEP 3: At death, stepped-up basis can wipe the gain for heirs, so it may never be taxed.
STEP 4: Homeowners already pay property tax on unrealized value every year.

CONCLUSION: If the gain is real enough to borrow against, it's real enough to tax. Workers pay tax on every paycheck.

PREMISE: The estate tax will hit billionaires' heirs hard.

STEP 1: The exemption is $15 million per person, $30 million per couple, from 2026.
STEP 2: Stepped-up basis can erase capital gains on inherited stock.
STEP 3: Trusts and planning shrink what's left to tax.
STEP 4: Meanwhile the Forbes 400 cutoff alone is $4.4 billion.

CONCLUSION: Dynasties are built on rules like these. The tracker shows the fortunes. The tax code shows why they stay.

PREMISE: Corporate tax cuts help workers, not billionaires.

STEP 1: Corporate tax receipts fell 16% in FY2026, from new write-offs in the 2025 law.
STEP 2: Corporate profits rose in 2026.
STEP 3: Higher profits lift stock prices. The richest 1% own about half of all stock, Fed data show.
STEP 4: Labor's share of business income fell to a record low.

CONCLUSION: Follow the cut: lower taxes, higher profits, higher stocks, richer owners. Workers' share went down.

PREMISE: Meta's Louisiana data center is a gift to Richland Parish.

STEP 1: Meta's Hyperion project started at $10 billion and grew to $50 billion in July 2026.
STEP 2: A Sherwood News analysis estimated about $3.3 billion in sales tax breaks on the original plan (estimate).
STEP 3: Meta projected more than 500 permanent jobs at first, now about 1,000.
STEP 4: On the original numbers, that's roughly $6.6 million in tax breaks per permanent job (estimate).

CONCLUSION: Count the cost per job. Jobs matter, but the deal is lopsided.

PREMISE: A tech billionaire's data center has nothing to do with my power bill.

STEP 1: Entergy Louisiana plans 10 gas plants for Meta's Hyperion site, about 7.5 gigawatts.
STEP 2: The governor says Meta pays for the base plants and customers save about $2.6 billion over 20 years.
STEP 3: A PSC commissioner and consumer advocates dispute that and warn ratepayers could be stuck if Meta leaves early.
STEP 4: U.S. electricity prices rose 3.8% in the past year.

CONCLUSION: Who carries the risk if the deal goes bad? Make it Meta, not the family paying the light bill.

PREMISE: Meta's tax break is small compared to the investment.

STEP 1: The estimated $3.3 billion sales tax break is small next to $50 billion of investment.
STEP 2: But compare it to Louisiana families: about $1.6 billion in SNAP benefits went out in the state over the past year.
STEP 3: The tax break equals about two years of all SNAP benefits in Louisiana.
STEP 4: Louisiana SNAP rolls fell about 21% in that year, mostly over paperwork.

CONCLUSION: Scale depends on what you compare it to. Next to hungry families, it's huge.

PREMISE: Louisiana's billionaires prove the state's economy works.

STEP 1: Forbes has listed three Louisiana billionaires: Todd Graves (Raising Cane's), Gayle Benson (Saints, Pelicans) and William Goldring (Sazerac).
STEP 2: Louisiana has the nation's highest poverty rate, 19.7% (official, 2023–2025).
STEP 3: Louisiana has no state minimum wage law.
STEP 4: A few large fortunes can sit beside widespread poverty.

CONCLUSION: A state can make billionaires and still fail its workers. Judge an economy by the bottom, not the top.

PREMISE: Billionaires earned it, so their wealth is none of our business.

STEP 1: Concede: Forbes rates 71% of the 2026 Forbes 400 as self-made.
STEP 2: Self-made fortunes still rely on public roads, public research, public schools and courts.
STEP 3: They also rely on workers whose share of income hit a record low.
STEP 4: Tax rules decide how much of that wealth gets taxed.

CONCLUSION: How a fortune was made doesn't settle what it owes. Public goods built it. Public rules shape it.

PREMISE: Billionaires create jobs, so taxing them kills jobs.

STEP 1: Some billionaires built companies that employ many people. That's real.
STEP 2: Jobs come from customers buying things, not from a founder's personal fortune growing.
STEP 3: The Forbes 400 gained $1.4 trillion, while employers added just 29,000 jobs in September.
STEP 4: Fortunes grew fast. Hiring didn't.

CONCLUSION: Demand creates jobs. Concentrated wealth mostly creates more wealth.

PREMISE: Walmart's owners are generous job creators.

STEP 1: Alice Walton was the world's richest woman at about $134 billion in March 2026, per Forbes.
STEP 2: A 2020 GAO report found Walmart among the top employers of workers on SNAP and Medicaid in the states it reviewed.
STEP 3: When pay is low, public programs fill the gap.
STEP 4: Those programs are now being cut.

CONCLUSION: Low wages plus public aid subsidize private fortunes. Cut the aid and workers lose twice.

PREMISE: Billionaire philanthropy makes up for low taxes.

STEP 1: Many billionaires give generously. That's good.
STEP 2: Giving is voluntary and often tax-deductible.
STEP 3: Donors pick the causes. Voters don't.
STEP 4: Public needs like Medicaid and SNAP are being cut while fortunes grow.

CONCLUSION: Charity is welcome, but it's not a substitute for fair taxes decided democratically.

PREMISE: Track their private jets and post where billionaires live.

STEP 1: No. Posting home addresses or tracking where people are is harassment and can get someone hurt.
STEP 2: It also hands opponents a reason to dismiss every real point.
STEP 3: Track what's public and relevant: net worth estimates, taxes, subsidies, lobbying and contracts.
STEP 4: The public record is damning enough.

CONCLUSION: Track wealth and power, not people's bodies. Follow the money, not the person home.

PREMISE: Make up a net worth for a billionaire if the real one isn't available.

STEP 1: No. Invented numbers destroy trust.
STEP 2: Use published estimates and name the source and date: Forbes, Bloomberg or a named analysis.
STEP 3: If there's no estimate, say so.
STEP 4: One fake number lets critics throw out every real one.

CONCLUSION: Real numbers only. Source and date every time.

PREMISE: Billionaires should run the government. They know how to get things done.

STEP 1: Running a company isn't running a democracy. A CEO answers to shareholders; officials answer to voters.
STEP 2: Billionaires have clear interests: lower taxes, fewer rules on their businesses.
STEP 3: A $908 billion fortune can outspend any community group.
STEP 4: Same standard for every party: billionaire influence on the left is a problem too.

CONCLUSION: Money is not a qualification. Power should answer to voters, not to wealth.

PREMISE: Trump is a billionaire, so the economy works for billionaires because of him.

STEP 1: Test it. Forbes estimated Trump's net worth fell to about $7 billion in 2026, from $7.3 billion.
STEP 2: Billionaire wealth overall soared, mostly from tech and AI stocks.
STEP 3: Tax law, stock markets and corporate power shaped that, across administrations of both parties.
STEP 4: One person doesn't explain a system.

CONCLUSION: Blame the rules and the system, not just one face. That's how you change it.

PREMISE: Taylor Swift is a billionaire, so billionaires are fine.

STEP 1: Forbes put her at about $2 billion in September, mostly from music and touring.
STEP 2: Some fortunes come from art fans choose to pay for. That's different from monopoly or political favors.
STEP 3: The issue isn't any single person. It's rules that let wealth pile up untaxed.
STEP 4: A fair tax applies the same way to a pop star and a tech founder.

CONCLUSION: Not every billionaire is a villain. Every fortune should play by the same tax rules.

PREMISE: The top 20 billionaires are just like the rest of the 400.

STEP 1: Forbes: the top 20 hold about half of the Forbes 400's $8 trillion.
STEP 2: Their combined wealth rose $970 billion in a year.
STEP 3: Musk alone leads the next-richest American by about $530 billion.
STEP 4: Even among the rich, wealth concentrates at the very top.

CONCLUSION: Inequality stacks: the top of the top pulls away fastest.

PREMISE: A billionaire's wealth comes from their own work.

STEP 1: A worker earning $37.81 an hour for 40 years earns about $3.1 million.
STEP 2: Musk's fortune is about 290,000 times that.
STEP 3: No one works 290,000 times harder.
STEP 4: Fortunes that size come from ownership: owning what others' work makes valuable.

CONCLUSION: Wages come from work. Fortunes come from ownership. That's why ownership rules matter.

PREMISE: Rising billionaire wealth trickles down to workers.

STEP 1: Forbes 400 wealth rose 21% in a year.
STEP 2: Real wages fell: pay up 3.0%, prices up 3.4%.
STEP 3: Credit card debt rose $21 billion in one quarter.
STEP 4: If wealth trickled down, workers wouldn't be borrowing to keep up.

CONCLUSION: The data shows wealth pooling at the top, not trickling down.

PREMISE: AI will make everyone richer.

STEP 1: Forbes counted 14 AI-linked newcomers on the 2026 Forbes 400 and at least 86 AI-linked billionaires worldwide in March.
STEP 2: Who owns the AI owns the gains.
STEP 3: Workers' share of income hit a record low the same year.
STEP 4: New technology can raise living standards if gains are shared through wages, taxes and public ownership.

CONCLUSION: AI can lift everyone or enrich a few. Ownership and policy decide which.

PREMISE: A wealth tax would just make billionaires leave.

STEP 1: Some might try. That's a real design problem.
STEP 2: U.S. citizens are taxed wherever they live, and exit taxes exist for those who renounce.
STEP 3: Enforcement funding and international cooperation matter.
STEP 4: Saying 'they'll leave' admits they hold power over our laws.

CONCLUSION: Design it well and enforce it. Don't let threats write tax policy.

PREMISE: The billionaire count rising shows America's success.

STEP 1: Concede: new companies and new technologies create real value.
STEP 2: But billionaires rose from about 3,000 worldwide to a record 3,428 in a year.
STEP 3: At home, SNAP fell 5.3 million people and Medicaid 5.1 million.
STEP 4: Success that leaves millions losing food and health aid isn't shared success.

CONCLUSION: Count both: the billionaires added and the families dropped.

PREMISE: Billionaires' wealth isn't real money, so it can't fund anything.

STEP 1: Stock can be sold, borrowed against or used as collateral.
STEP 2: Forbes 400 fortunes are estimated from market prices that buyers actually pay.
STEP 3: Billionaires use that wealth to buy companies, media and political influence.
STEP 4: If it can buy a social network, it can pay a fair tax.

CONCLUSION: Wealth that buys power is real enough to tax.

PREMISE: Workers who complain about billionaires are just jealous.

STEP 1: This isn't about envy. It's about rules.
STEP 2: Workers pay payroll tax on every dollar. Billionaire gains can go untaxed for life.
STEP 3: Public aid is shrinking while fortunes grow.
STEP 4: Asking for the same rules isn't jealousy. It's fairness.

CONCLUSION: Name the rule, not the feeling. Same rules for everyone.

PREMISE: Musk's fortune came from building great companies, so it's all deserved.

STEP 1: Tesla and SpaceX are real companies with real achievements. Say so.
STEP 2: Tesla benefited from government EV credits and regulatory credit sales. SpaceX has large NASA and defense contracts.
STEP 3: Public money and public policy helped build those fortunes.
STEP 4: The public should share in what it helped create.

CONCLUSION: Credit the work. Count the public's investment too.

PREMISE: A billionaire minimum tax is radical.

STEP 1: The 1950s top income tax rate was 91%. Today's is 37%.
STEP 2: A minimum tax would ask billionaires to pay at least a set rate on their gains.
STEP 3: Workers already pay a minimum: payroll tax on every dollar, no exceptions.
STEP 4: Asking the richest for a floor isn't radical. It's catching up.

CONCLUSION: Workers have a tax floor. Billionaires should too.

PREMISE: Social Security is going broke because people live longer.

STEP 1: Longer lives and fewer workers per retiree are real pressures.
STEP 2: Payroll tax stops at $184,500 in wages.
STEP 3: A billionaire's salary passes the cap early in the year, if they take a salary at all. Their stock gains pay nothing in.
STEP 4: Lifting the cap closes much of the shortfall.

CONCLUSION: Social Security isn't broke. It's capped. Billionaires stop paying before workers do.

PREMISE: Billionaires are too busy to influence politics.

STEP 1: Wealth buys ads, lobbyists, think tanks and media platforms.
STEP 2: Billionaires on the left and right fund campaigns and causes.
STEP 3: The 2025 tax law cut corporate taxes and expanded estate exemptions.
STEP 4: Policy outcomes tend to track the interests of those who fund them.

CONCLUSION: Follow the money from donor to law. That holds for both parties.

PREMISE: Raising Cane's founder made billions selling chicken fingers. Good for him.

STEP 1: Todd Graves built a real business from Baton Rouge. That's a genuine success.
STEP 2: Forbes estimated his fortune at about $22 billion.
STEP 3: Fast food workers in Louisiana start from a $7.25 legal floor, though many chains pay more.
STEP 4: Celebrate the business and still ask how its profits are shared with the crew.

CONCLUSION: Respect the builder. Organize the workers. Both can be true.

PREMISE: The billionaire tracker is just leftist propaganda.

STEP 1: The numbers come from Forbes, a pro-business magazine, and the Federal Reserve.
STEP 2: Advocacy groups like Americans for Tax Fairness are labeled as such.
STEP 3: The tracker includes good news: the bottom half's wealth rose 7% in a year.
STEP 4: Facts don't become propaganda because they're uncomfortable.

CONCLUSION: Use mainstream and official sources, label advocates, admit good news. That's how you earn trust.

PREMISE: Billionaires got rich, poor people got poorer.

STEP 1: Check it. The bottom half's net worth actually rose about 7% in a year.
STEP 2: But it rose far less in dollars: $0.28 trillion vs $8.75 trillion for the top 1%.
STEP 3: And real wages fell, while millions lost SNAP and Medicaid.
STEP 4: Precise wording: the poor gained a little in wealth while losing ground on pay and aid; the rich gained enormously.

CONCLUSION: Be exact. 'The gap grew' is true. 'The poor got poorer in wealth' isn't.
sources: Federal Reserve DFA via FRED, Q2 2026

text:
PREMISE: Every billionaire is a policy failure.

STEP 1: That's a slogan. Test it.
STEP 2: Some fortunes come from inventions people value.
STEP 3: The policy failure is in the rules: untaxed gains, stepped-up basis, low capital gains rates, weak antitrust.
STEP 4: Fix the rules and fewer fortunes grow unchecked.

CONCLUSION: Aim at the rules that make fortunes untouchable, not just the slogan.

PREMISE: A tax on billionaires won't help Louisiana.

STEP 1: Federal dollars fund most SNAP benefits and much of Medicaid in Louisiana.
STEP 2: Louisiana SNAP benefits totaled about $1.6 billion over the past year, all federal.
STEP 3: Those programs are shrinking for budget reasons.
STEP 4: Federal revenue from the richest could protect them.

CONCLUSION: Billionaire taxes are a Louisiana kitchen-table issue. Federal money feeds Louisiana families.

PREMISE: The 590 billionaires who missed the Forbes 400 show wealth is spreading.

STEP 1: 590 billionaires missed the cutoff, up from 500.
STEP 2: The cutoff rose to a record $4.4 billion.
STEP 3: More billionaires means wealth is spreading among the rich, not to workers.
STEP 4: The bottom half still holds 2.3% of wealth.

CONCLUSION: Wealth spreading from billionaires to other billionaires isn't spreading to us.

PREMISE: Interest on the debt and billionaires are unrelated.

STEP 1: Net interest cost $1.143 trillion in FY2026, more than defense.
STEP 2: Tax cuts that mostly benefit the top add to borrowing.
STEP 3: Interest goes to bondholders. The wealthiest households own a large share of bonds and other financial assets.
STEP 4: So tax cuts at the top can return to the top again as interest.

CONCLUSION: Cut their taxes, borrow the difference, pay them interest. Follow that loop.

PREMISE: Billionaire wealth is so big it's meaningless to compare.

STEP 1: Make it concrete.
STEP 2: The Forbes 400's one-year gain of $1.4 trillion is about 70% of this year's federal deficit.
STEP 3: It's more than ten times what the government spent on food programs.
STEP 4: It's about 16 million median household incomes.

CONCLUSION: Translate billions into budgets and households. That's how people feel the scale.

PREMISE: Billionaires take big risks, so they deserve big rewards.

STEP 1: Risk is real. Fortunes swing: Musk was about $1.285 trillion in June and $908 billion in September (different sources).
STEP 2: The two estimates differ by about $377 billion. Either way, he was the richest American by far.
STEP 3: A worker who loses a job can lose their income and health insurance at once.
STEP 4: Unemployment rose to 4.2% in September while Medicaid shrank by 5.1 million.

CONCLUSION: A billionaire's bad quarter still leaves billions. A worker's bad month can mean losing the house. Risk isn't shared equally.

PREMISE: Workers should focus on their own jobs, not billionaires.

STEP 1: Workers' share of income hit a record low.
STEP 2: Billionaire wealth hit a record high.
STEP 3: Those are two sides of one ledger: what's not paid in wages flows to owners.
STEP 4: Organizing raises wages. Tax policy shapes what's left at the top.

CONCLUSION: Your paycheck and their fortune are connected. Fight on both fronts.

PREMISE: We should just ignore billionaires and focus on the poor.

STEP 1: Poverty policy needs money.
STEP 2: Congress cut SNAP and Medicaid while lowering corporate taxes.
STEP 3: The richest gained over a trillion dollars in a year.
STEP 4: You can't fund the floor without asking something of the top.

CONCLUSION: Helping the poor and taxing the rich are one plan, not two.

PREMISE: Run the billionaire tracker every year and nothing changes.

STEP 1: Tracking alone doesn't change laws. Organizing does.
STEP 2: The numbers give people a shared fact base.
STEP 3: Ballot measures and organized workers have raised wages and expanded Medicaid in red states.
STEP 4: Data plus organizing is how rules change.

CONCLUSION: Track it, share it, organize around it. Numbers are the map; people are the movement.
